content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a method of learning classification and segmentation in compressed domain via architecture modification and knowledge transferring. It avoids reconstructing the image and achieves comparable or even higher recognition/segmentation accuracy. On both tasks, the proposed method shows interesting gain over the pixel-domain approach or the other two existing methods.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths: 
(1) The paper is well-organized, with a clear description of the proposed method.
(2) The proposed method is simple and straightforward, and it provides an attractive alternative to performing machine vision tasks with compressed images.
(3) Clear performance gain as compared to the baseline and the existing methods under the authors’ experimental setting.

Weaknesses:
(1) The novelty of the proposed method is limited. The claimed novelty lies in two parts: (a) modifying the existing recognition network and (b) introducing a knowledge transfer loss. The gain of (a) is unclear, and a similar idea appears in [1]. For (b), [2] also adopts a similar approach. Furthermore, knowledge distillation itself is nothing new; the adaptation of it to this task also seems straightforward.
[1] Z. Wang et. al. “Learning from the CNN-Based Compressed Domain,” WACV 2022.
[2] Y. Matsubara et. al. “Supervised Compression for Resource-Constrained Edge Computing Systems,” WACV 2022.
(2) The comparison with the existing methods in Fig. 5 may not be fair. The codecs used by the three competing methods are different. It essentially means learning from different input data. 
(3) It would be interesting to see whether the same knowledge transfer loss can work well on the network architectures of the other existing methods.
(4) The two learned codecs used in experiments, Hyperprior and Hyperprior-context, are quite similar, with the same analysis/synthesis transform design. The generalization ability is hard to discern with such setup. Perhaps a codec with different transform design, e.g. transformer-based transform coding, ICLR 2022, should be adopted.
(5) More insights into why the compressed-domain recognition achieves higher accuracy than the pixel-domain recognition should be provided. 
(6) It is necessary to address or comment on the complexity of the other competing methods.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is well-organized and easy to follow. But, the novelty appears limited. The description includes enough implementation details. As such, the proposed method should be reproducible.
content.summary_of_the_review: The novelty of the proposed method is limited. Similar ideas have been proposed before. The comparison with the existing methods may not be fair. Also, the use of two highly similar codecs to test the generalizability of the proposed method is not convincing. Also, more insights into why the compressed-domain recognition performs better than the pixel-domain recognition should be provided.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 1: The contributions are neither significant nor novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.confidence: 5: You are absolutely certain about your assessment. You are very familiar with the related work and checked the math/other details carefully.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper considers the problem of executing computer vision tasks in the compressed domain of learned image coders. A knowledge transfer loss is applied to the intermediate features of the compressed domain model, improving the task accuracy of both classification and instance segmentation. Experiments show that the proposed method achieves better classification accuracy than previous methods.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength

- The network architecture and loss function is well explained.
- It is shown that compressed domain task accuracy can exceed the reconstructed pixel domain task accuracy, which is very interesting and promising.
- The proposed method outperforms previous ones in the same setting.



Major Weakness:
- The proposed method is not new. Cross-modal knowledge transfer has already been well-studied [1]. The application of pixel-to-compressed domain transfer loss has also been presented in a similar setting [2].

[1] Gupta, Saurabh, Judy Hoffman, and Jitendra Malik. "Cross-modal distillation for supervision transfer." Proceedings of the IEEE conference on computer vision and pattern recognition. 2016.
[2] Matsubara, Yoshitomo, et al. "Supervised compression for resource-constrained edge computing systems." Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF Winter Conference on Applications of Computer Vision. 2022.


Minor Weakness:
1. The notation used in Sec. 3.2.2 is confusing to me:
-- The symbol $p$ is used to denote both the "pixel domain" and "class predictions".
-- The symbol $C$ is used to denote both "convolution" as in $f_{C5}$, and "the total number of classes".
-- $p$ and $c$ are placed as superscripts, indistinguishable from the exponential notation.
An example for improving the notation:
-- Use another symbol, for example, $N$, for the number of classes.
-- Use $C_5$, $C'_5$, $P_5$, and $P'_5$ instead of $f^c_{C5}$, $f^p_{C5}$, $f^c_{P5}$, and $f^p_{P5}$ respectively. Similar rules apply to the terms in Eq. (2).
-- The subscripts $i,j$ in Eq. (1) could be avoided by using expectations instead of summations.

2. It is not clear how the pixel domain experiment in Figure 3 is conducted. There are several possibilities: a) the pre-trained ResNet-50, without any further training/finetuning, is evaluated on reconstructed ImageNet val set; b) the pre-trained ResNet-50 is first finetuned on reconstructed ImageNet training images and then evaluated on reconstructed ImageNet val set; c) the ResNet-50 is trained from scratch (ie, random initialization) on reconstructed ImageNet training images and then evaluated on reconstructed ImageNet val set. Such a setting is essential but is missing from the paper.

3. The same question as above also holds for the instance segmentation experiments in Figure 4.

4. It would be great if a) the top-1 accuracy of the pre-trained ResNet-50, and b) the mask mAP of the pre-trained Mask RCNN can be reported for reference.

5. The complexity analysis provided in Table 2 is not convincing. To my best understanding, Table 2 implicitly assumes that the quantized feature $\hat{y}$ is already available, without considering the cost of entropy decoding. The entropy decoding could be expensive, e.g., for the hyperprior-context model. In my humble opinion, a) one should consider the end-to-end complexity from decoding the bits to the class/segmentation prediction, and b) a number of network parameters, CPU, and/or GPU latency should also be reported in addition to FLOPs.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: Results are eye-catching, but it is not clear how to obtain these. A  clear description of the experiments is highly desired, especially how to use the knowledge transfer to improve the accuracy.
content.summary_of_the_review: My main concern lies in the contribution of the paper, as the method of (cross-modal) knowledge transfer has been studied in a number of works in literature (see Major Weakness). What is new in this paper is its application to the specific setting of task inference with a pre-trained image compression model. I consider the experimental results attractive to the research community, but the method is not. Unless the authors could provide a clear description of the novelty and difference of the proposed approach in contrast to [2], I would suggest a weak rejection.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes a compressed-domain learning method of an end-to-end image compression model to achieve comparable performance to pixel-domain methods. Because the compressed-domain features would miss inductive biases in the pixel domain, the authors proposed a knowledge transfer loss to narrow the gap between compressed domain and pixel domain. The performance of the proposed method has been evaluated in image classification tasks and image segmentation, using ResNet-50 architecture (and MaskRCNN). For each task, the compressed latent representations from two image compression models have been employed.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength : The paper presents an idea that the knowledge transfer of pixel-domain to compressed-domain can help provide comparable performance in vision tasks. The proposed method also provides robust features to compression artifacts, which has been demonstrated in Section 5. The performance evaluations are conducted for image classifications and instance segmentation.

Weakness : The experimental conditions would not be properly set up for fair comparisons. The ablation tests are limited to show where the performance comes from.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
1. The reviewer has some questions of the experimental configuration. Considering the contribution of this study is transferring knowledge from pixel-domain CNN into compressed-domain CNN, it would be fair comparisons to use the same architectures for compressed-domain CNN (and the same compression model) as the compared methods, e.g. in Figure 5. Otherwise, it is ambiguous if the proposed method properly improve performance as compared to the competing methods.  

2. The performance of the pixel-domain model presented in Figure 3-4 is not clearly described; is it trained using reconstructed images only or using both original and reconstructed images? Assuming it is trained using only the reconstructed images and denoting it as a pixel-domain model-test, the authors should clarify whether a pixel-domain CNN presented in Figure 1 is a different model with the tested model and the performance comes solely from the transfer learning.

3. The reviewer was curious why both original and reconstructed images are input to the pixel-domain CNN during the training of the compressed-domain CNN. The authors should discuss the reasons and conduct ablation tests by inputting one or both images an original image or reconstructed image or both, as input to the pixel-domain CNN during the learning of compressed-domain CNN.

4. In the feature loss function, a further consideration is required because the feature f_c and f_p would show different distribution as different input.

5. How the proposed method can be expanded arbitrary networks? The proposed method is somewhat limited to specific architectures because  several specific features (and layers) have been used for engineering and the knowledge transferring is somewhat simple. 

Minor comments
1. Some example images can be provided to see the performance of the segmentation with respect to bpp.
2.  The authors are encouraged to improve the mathematical notations. The notations can be included to Figure 1.
content.summary_of_the_review: Although the paper presents an interesting idea of enhancing compressed-domain features, the experiments would lack sufficient considerations of experimental configurations and ablation tests. The proposed method is somewhat limited to specific layers of network architectures.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
